facts.fact: Qutb-ud-din Aibak was the first Sultan of Delhi and founded the Slave dynasty in 1206.
Aibak was called 'Lakh Baksh' for his generosity.
Aibak began the Qutb Minar, named after the saint Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.
Aibak died in a fall while playing chaugan (polo) at Lahore.
Iltutmish introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital.
Iltutmish organised the iqta system.
Iltutmish formed the Turkan-i-Chihalgani (the Forty).
Razia Sultana was the first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.
Razia married Malik Altunia to regain her throne.
Balban introduced sijda and paibos and followed a policy of blood and iron.
Jalaluddin Khalji founded the Khalji dynasty in 1290 and made Kilokhri his capital.
Alauddin Khalji killed his uncle Jalaluddin in 1296 and seized the throne.
Alauddin conquered Gujarat, Ranthambore, Chittor and Malwa.
Malik Kafur led Alauddin's Deccan campaigns against Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai.
Alauddin's cloth and general market was called the Sarai Adl.
The Shahna-i-Mandi supervised Alauddin's markets.
The Diwan-i-Riyasat registered every merchant.
Alauddin kept a cash-paid standing army with the Dagh and Chehra system.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the Tughlaq dynasty (1320) and built Tughlaqabad.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a token currency of copper coins.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised taxes in the Doab.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq planned expeditions to Khurasan and Qarachil.
Firoz Shah set up the Dar-ul-Shafa (hospital) and Diwan-i-Khairat (marriage bureau).
Firoz Shah imposed jizya on Brahmins.
Firoz founded Firozabad, Hissar and Jaunpur.
Timur sacked Delhi in 1398 during the Tughlaq period.
Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414 and took the title Rayat-i-Ala.
Bahlol Lodi replaced the last Sayyid, Alam Shah, in 1451.
Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra.
Ibrahim Lodi was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).
Five dynasties ruled in turn: Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.
At the Second Battle of Tarain (1192) Ghuri defeated Prithviraj; at Chandawar (1194) he defeated Jaichandra.
Bakhtiyar Khalji overran Bihar and Bengal.
Alauddin Khalji built the Alai Darwaza (1311).
Ziauddin Barani wrote the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi.
Minhaj-us-Siraj wrote the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.
The iqta was a non-hereditary assignment of revenue to a muqti who kept troops.
Key central departments were the Diwan-i-Wizarat, Diwan-i-Arz and Diwan-i-Insha.
Aibak built the Adhai-din-ka-Jhonpra at Ajmer.
Iltutmish built the Hauz-i-Shamsi.
Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 712 CE for the Umayyad Caliphate.
Muhammad bin Qasim defeated Dahir, king of Sindh, after taking the port of Debal.
The Chachnama is the Persian history of the Arab conquest of Sindh.
Further Arab advances were stopped by Nagabhata I (Pratihara), Bappa Rawal of Mewar and the Chalukyas.
Sabuktigin, the real founder of Ghaznavid power, defeated the Hindushahi king Jayapala.
Mahmud of Ghazni (998–1030) raided India 17 times between 1000 and 1027.
Alberuni came with Mahmud and wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind).
Firdausi wrote the Shahnama at Mahmud of Ghazni's court.
Utbi's Tarikh-i-Yamini is a history of Mahmud's reign.
Muhammad Ghori (Muizzuddin Muhammad bin Sam) took Ghazni in 1173 and entered India by the Gomal Pass, taking Multan (1175).
Ghori took Lahore from the last Ghaznavid, Khusrau Malik, in 1186.
The Ghori–Prithviraj conflict began over the fort of Bhatinda (Tabarhind).
Superior Turkish cavalry, speed and organisation decided the Second Battle of Tarain.
Bakhtiyar Khalji took Nadia, capital of the Sena king Lakshmana Sena, by a surprise raid (c.1204).
Bakhtiyar Khalji destroyed Nalanda and Vikramshila (c.1193–1200).
Ghori was routed by the Khwarizm Shah at Andkhud (1204), turning Turkish attention fully to India.
Muhammad Ghori was killed in 1206 at Damyak by the Khokhars.
Ghori's slave-generals Aibak (Delhi), Yalduz (Ghazni) and Qubacha (Multan) divided his empire.
Iltutmish defeated Aram Shah near Delhi (the battle of Jud) in 1211.
Iltutmish belonged to the Ilbari tribe of Turks.
Iltutmish defeated Yalduz at Tarain in 1216 (sometimes called the third battle of Tarain).
Iltutmish refused shelter to Jalaluddin Mangbarni, saving Delhi from Chengiz Khan (1221).
Iltutmish received a letter of investiture from the Abbasid Caliph in 1229.
Sultan Ghari, built by Iltutmish for his son Nasiruddin Mahmud, is the first Islamic tomb in India.
Razia appointed the Abyssinian Jamaluddin Yaqut as master of the royal stables (amir-i-akhur), angering the Turkish nobles.
Under Bahram Shah the nobles created the post of Naib-i-Mamlakat (regent).
Nasiruddin Mahmud (1246–1265) led a simple life copying the Quran; Minhaj dedicated the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri to him.
Balban created the military department Diwan-i-Arz.
Balban introduced the Persian festival of Nauroz at court.
Balban's son Prince Muhammad, patron of Amir Khusrau, was killed fighting the Mongols (1285).
Kaiqubad built the palace-town of Kilokhri on the Yamuna, later used by Jalaluddin Khalji.
Jalaluddin allowed Mongol settlers who accepted Islam to live near Delhi; they were called "New Muslims".
Alauddin Khalji took the title 'Sikandar-i-Sani' (the second Alexander).
Malik Kafur, called 'Hazardinari', was captured at Cambay during the Gujarat campaign (1299).
Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan led the 1299 Gujarat campaign against Karna Vaghela.
Ranthambore (1301) was held by the Chauhan Hammir Deva.
Chittor (1303) was ruled by Rana Ratan Singh; the Padmini story comes from Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Padmavat (1540).
Alauddin built Siri fort (c.1303) as a defence against the Mongols; it was the second city of Delhi.
Alauddin fixed the land revenue at half the produce, assessed by measurement.
Alauddin levied a house tax (ghari) and a grazing tax (charai).
Alauddin set up the Diwan-i-Mustakhraj to recover revenue arrears.
Alauddin curbed the privileges of the khuts, muqaddams and chaudharis (rural intermediaries).
Malik Kafur's raids were Devagiri (1307–08), Warangal (1309–10), Dwarasamudra (1311) and Madurai (1311).
At Madurai Malik Kafur intervened in the civil war of the Pandya brothers Vira and Sundara Pandya.
Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah Khalji was the only Delhi Sultan to call himself Khalifa (Caliph).
Khusrau Khan, a convert of the Baradu (Barwari) group, killed Mubarak Shah and ruled briefly as Nasiruddin (1320).
Alauddin built the Hauz-i-Alai (Hauz Khas) tank and began the unfinished Alai Minar.
Amir Khusrau was called 'Tuti-i-Hind' (Parrot of India).
Amir Khusrau is credited with developing the qawwali (and, by tradition, the sitar and tabla).
Amir Khusrau was a disciple of the Chishti saint Nizamuddin Auliya.
Amir Khusrau wrote the Qiran-us-Sadain on the meeting of Kaiqubad and his father Bughra Khan.
Amir Khusrau wrote the Miftah-ul-Futuh on Jalaluddin Khalji's victories.
Amir Khusrau's Ashiqa tells the love story of Khizr Khan and Deval Rani.
Amir Khusrau's Nuh Sipihr praises India and Mubarak Shah's reign.
Amir Khusrau's Tughlaq Nama celebrates Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's rise.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq was earlier called Ghazi Malik and was governor of Dipalpur.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq is credited by Barani as the first Sultan to dig canals for irrigation.
Ghiyasuddin died in 1325 when a pavilion at Afghanpur collapsed on him.
Nizamuddin Auliya's saying 'Hunuz Dilli dur ast' (Delhi is yet far) is linked to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved the capital to Daulatabad in 1327.
The token currency (bronze/copper) was issued in 1329–30.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq created the Diwan-i-Kohi, a department of agriculture.
Agricultural loans (taccavi or sondhar) were given under Muhammad bin Tughlaq and withdrawn by Firoz.
The Qarachil expedition was sent into the Kumaon hills (Himalaya) and was destroyed.
For the Khurasan plan Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised an army of 3,70,000 and then disbanded it.
Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan, came in 1333, served as qazi of Delhi and was sent as envoy to China (1342).
Muhammad bin Tughlaq built Jahanpanah, the fourth city of Delhi, with the Bijai Mandal.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq died at Thatta in Sindh (1351) while chasing a rebel.
In his reign Madurai (1335), Vijayanagara (1336), Bengal (1338) and the Bahmani kingdom (1347) broke away.
Firoz Shah created the Diwan-i-Bandagan, a department of slaves (about 1,80,000).
Firoz Shah set up the Diwan-i-Istihqaq for pensions and aid to the poor.
Firoz collected only the four Sharia taxes: kharaj, khams, jizya and zakat.
Firoz levied an irrigation tax (haq-i-sharb) of one-tenth on lands watered by his canals.
Firoz's longest canal ran from the Yamuna to Hissar (the forerunner of the Western Yamuna canal).
Firoz brought Ashokan pillars from Topra (Ambala) and Meerut to Delhi.
Sanskrit works from the Jwalamukhi (Nagarkot) temple library were translated into Persian as the Dalail-i-Firoz Shahi.
Shams-i-Siraj Afif also wrote a Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, on Firoz's reign.
Ziauddin Barani wrote the Fatawa-i-Jahandari on statecraft.
Firoz attacked Jajnagar (Odisha) and desecrated the Jagannath temple at Puri.
Firoz founded Firozabad, Hissar, Jaunpur and Fatehabad.
Firoz Shah repaired the top storeys of the Qutb Minar after a lightning strike (1368).
Timur invaded in 1398 during the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah Tughlaq.
Timur was the ruler of Samarqand; his memoir is the Malfuzat-i-Timuri.
Malik Sarwar (Malik-us-Sharq) founded the Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur in 1394.
Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi wrote the Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi on the Sayyid period.
Muhammad Shah Sayyid's octagonal tomb stands in the Lodi Gardens.
The last Sayyid, Alam Shah, retired to Badaun and gave Delhi up to Bahlol Lodi (1451).
Bahlol Lodi issued the copper coin called Bahloli.
Bahlol Lodi annexed the Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur.
Sikandar Lodi wrote Persian verse under the pen-name 'Gulrukhi'.
Sikandar Lodi introduced the Gaz-i-Sikandari, a measuring yard of 39 digits (about 30 inches).
Sikandar Lodi's tomb is the first garden tomb in India and has a double dome.
Ibrahim Lodi was defeated by Rana Sanga of Mewar at Khatoli (c.1517–18).
Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of Punjab, and Alam Khan invited Babur to invade.
Ibrahim Lodi was the only Delhi Sultan to die on the battlefield (Panipat, 21 April 1526).
The Lodis were the first Afghan dynasty to rule Delhi.
The Diwan-i-Wizarat (finance) was headed by the wazir.
The Diwan-i-Insha (royal correspondence) was headed by the dabir-i-mamalik.
The Diwan-i-Risalat dealt with religious affairs and was headed by the sadr-us-sudur.
The Diwan-i-Qaza (justice) was headed by the qazi-ul-quzat.
The barid-i-mamalik headed the state intelligence and news service.
The mustaufi-i-mamalik was the auditor-general and the mushrif-i-mamalik the accountant-general.
Provinces were divided into shiqs (districts) under shiqdars, and shiqs into parganas.
At village level the muqaddam (headman), chaudhari and patwari (record-keeper) served the state.
Khalisa was crown land whose revenue went directly to the Sultan's treasury.
The Sultanate iqta was the forerunner of the Mughal jagir; neither was meant to be hereditary.
Zakat was a religious tax on Muslims (about 2.5% of wealth).
Khams was the state share of war booty — one-fifth by law (Alauddin took four-fifths).
Iltutmish's silver tanka weighed about 175 grains.
The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque at Delhi, begun by Aibak, used material from 27 temples.
The Qutb Minar and its monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.
The Qutb Minar has five storeys and stands about 72.5 metres high.
Balban's tomb at Mehrauli has the first true arch in India; the Alai Darwaza has the first true dome.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb has sloping (battered) walls — a Tughlaq feature.
Lodi-period tombs are octagonal or square; Sayyid and Lodi tombs fill the Lodi Gardens.
The seven cities of Delhi are Qila Rai Pithora (Lal Kot), Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad, Dinpanah (Purana Qila) and Shahjahanabad.
Hasan Nizami wrote the Taj-ul-Maasir on the reign of Aibak.
Isami wrote the Futuh-us-Salatin, a verse history, at the Bahmani court.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq wrote his own account, the Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi.
Amir Khusrau's Khazain-ul-Futuh describes Alauddin Khalji's conquests.
Ibn Battuta's travel book is the Rihla (Kitab-ul-Rihla).
